opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the key shift is where the improvement can happen. For a long time, when people talked about recursive self-improvement, they pictured a model rewriting its own weights: the system somehow retrains itself into something smarter. That's an enormously expensive, slow, high-stakes loop. You need a training run, evals, and a lot of compute, and the feedback cycle is measured in weeks or months.

The harness changes that. It's the scaffolding around the model: the prompts, the tools, the memory, how it plans, how it checks its own work, how it recovers from errors. All of that is just code and text, and models are now quite good at reading and writing code and text. So you get a loop where the agent runs on a task, you look at the traces of where it failed, and then the agent itself proposes changes to its own harness. Maybe it adds a verification step, writes a new tool, or restructures how it decomposes problems. Then you rerun and measure. That cycle can be minutes or hours, not months, and it's cheap enough to run many times.

The other piece is that the models crossed a capability threshold where they can actually do this usefully. A couple of years ago, if you asked a model to improve its own scaffolding, you mostly got plausible-sounding changes that didn't move the numbers. Now the models are good enough at software engineering and at diagnosing their own failure modes that the edits are frequently real improvements. And critically, we have benchmarks and task environments with fairly objective signals, like tests passing or tasks completing, so you can tell whether a change helped rather than just trusting the model's opinion of itself.

I'd add one caveat, though. This is self-improvement of the system, not necessarily of the underlying intelligence. The harness can unlock a lot of latent capability, and those gains compound, but there's probably a ceiling set by the base model. The really interesting question is what happens when those harness improvements start feeding back into how we generate training data and train the next model. That's when the loop closes more fully, and I think we're starting to see the early versions of that now.

r001.rationale: It describes the harness as code and text and says the model can read and write that material, establishing code as a medium for both the agent’s work and harness changes.

r002.rationale: It calls weight-based self-revision expensive and slow, but does not explain that a trillion-parameter model’s weights are too large to fit into its own context.

r003.rationale: It says the agent can inspect failures and propose changes to its own harness, including adding tools and changing task decomposition.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest framing is that recursive self-improvement didn't get unlocked by a jump in raw model capability. It got unlocked by where the leverage moved. For a long time, if you wanted the model to get better, the only lever you really had was training. And training is slow, expensive, and controlled by a small number of people who touch the weights. The model can't participate in that loop in any meaningful way. It can't run a pretraining job on itself on a Tuesday afternoon.

What changed is that a huge fraction of what makes an agent actually good in practice now lives outside the weights. It's in the harness. It's the tool definitions, the way context gets assembled and compacted, the retry logic, how you decompose a task into subagents, what gets checked before an edit lands, how memory persists across sessions. If you take the same frozen model and put it in two different harnesses, the gap in real-world performance can be bigger than the gap between two model generations. That's the thing people underestimate.

And the harness is just code. It's text in a repo. Which means the model can read it, reason about it, propose changes, run evals on those changes, and ship them. That's the loop. Not the model rewriting its own weights, but the model improving the scaffolding that determines how effectively its existing capability gets applied. And that loop can run on the order of hours instead of months.

The second piece is that the harness is where the feedback signal lives. When an agent fails a task, the failure usually isn't "the model was too dumb." It's "the model didn't have the right tool," or "the context window got polluted," or "it didn't verify before claiming it was done." Those are legible, diagnosable, fixable failures. You can write a test that captures the failure mode, change the harness, and watch the test pass. The model can do that whole thing itself. So you get this tight, verifiable, low-cost improvement cycle that just wasn't structurally possible when all the capability lived in opaque parameters.

I'd also say there's a flywheel between the layers. Once the harness is good enough that the agent can reliably do multi-hour engineering work, one of the things it can do is engineering work on training infrastructure, on eval suites, on data pipelines. So the harness improvement feeds back into the slower weight-level loop too. It doesn't replace it, it accelerates it.

Now, the caveat I'd put on all of this is that "recursive" is doing a lot of work in that phrase. What we actually have today is a loop with humans still deciding which harness changes merge, and evals that are good but not perfect. The recursion is real but it's gated. The interesting question over the next year or two is how much of that gating is load-bearing for safety versus just friction, and I don't think anyone has a clean answer yet. But the reason it's even a live question now, rather than science fiction, is that the thing being improved finally became something the model can read and edit.

r001.rationale: It identifies the harness as code the model can read and change, but does not identify code as the shared medium of both the agent’s outputs and its harness.

r002.rationale: It says the model cannot rewrite its weights and contrasts training with harness changes, but does not mention trillion-parameter weights being too large to fit into its context for direct revision.

r003.rationale: It explains that the model can read, propose changes to, evaluate, and ship changes to the harness code that governs its behavior.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that an agent can improve the system around the model without having to change the model’s weights. The harness is code: it controls what tools the model can use, what context it gets, how it checks its work, and when it keeps going. Those are things a coding agent can inspect and modify.

So you can build a loop where the agent attempts a task, looks at where it failed, changes the harness, and runs the evaluation again. If that change makes it better at coding or debugging, it may also become better at making the next change to its own harness. That’s the recursive part.

What’s different now is that models are capable enough to do more of that work end to end, and more of the machinery governing their behavior is accessible as software. But the feedback signal is critical. You need to establish that a change actually improves performance across tasks, rather than just helping on the example it was looking at. The harness makes the loop possible; reliable evaluation is what makes it useful.

r001.rationale: The response calls the harness code and says a coding agent can modify it, but does not state that code is the shared medium of both the agent’s outputs and the harness.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss trillion-parameter model weights or why they are too large to include in context for direct self-revision.

r003.rationale: It explains that the agent can inspect and change its harness code, then use improved coding ability to make further changes to that harness.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that the harness gives the model something it can actually change. If improvement requires retraining the underlying model, you need a whole training pipeline. But an agent’s behavior also depends on its instructions, the tools it has, how it manages context, and how it checks its work. Those are things an agent can potentially inspect and modify through code.

So you can start to close the loop: attempt a task, look at where it failed, change the harness, and run it again. The same coding capabilities that let the agent work on your software can let it work on the software running itself.

The caveat is that making a change isn’t the same as improving. You need an evaluation that tells you whether the change actually helped, ideally on tasks beyond the one that motivated it. But the harness makes that feedback loop much more accessible. You don’t have to change the model’s weights to improve the system around it.

r001.rationale: The response says an agent can modify its harness through code, but does not identify code as the shared medium for both the agent’s outputs and the harness that runs it.

r002.rationale: It does not mention trillion-parameter model weights or explain why they are too large to place in the model’s context for direct self-revision.

r003.rationale: It explains that an agent can inspect and modify its harness through code, then rerun it, making recursive improvement possible.
